text.p: Austrian banking was turned on its head on Wednesday as reports grew that market leader Bank Austria poised to make a bid for its nearest rival Creditanstalt-Bankverein.
A source close to Bank Austria's supervisory board privately confirmed media reports of a planned 16 billion schillings ($1.5 billion) takeover of privatisation candidate Creditanstalt.
"The headlines are not wrong," the source told Reuters ahead of a meeting of the Bank Austria board on Wednesday afternoon.
Bank Austria spokesman Heimo Hackel confirmed that Creditanstalt figured on the agenda and said an announcement was likely in the early evening.
Bank Austria shares were suspended from trade in Vienna, Frankfurt and Brussels.

Tabloid daily Neue Kronen Zeitung reported that Bank Austria, majority owned by the City of Vienna, was poised to bid 804 schillings for each of the government's 19.9 million Creditanstalt shares, representing 70 percent of voting stock.
That is well above the market price of 721 schillings and a 720-730 schillings bid lodged by an international consortium led by EA-Generali.
Creditanstalt, once banker to the Habsburg rulers of the Austro-Hungarian empire, gave notice it would not become an easy target for Bank Austria, however.

"This plan will destroy an attractive bank and open the door to foreigners. It is not a privatisation but under the guise of a privatisation will polarise the whole of Austria's banking sector," said one bank executive, talking on condition of anonymity.

The Austrian government has been trying to sell its Creditanstalt stake without success since 1990, making it one of Austria's longest-running privatisation sagas. Efforts to secure a sale have always fallen apart on reluctance to entertain foreign bids.
News of an expected bid took analysts by surprise.
"If the price is correct, it is fairly meaty in relation to the EA-Generali bid and the market price," said Victoria Maxwell, an analyst at James Capel in London.
She forecast Finance Minister Viktor Klima, desperate to raise fresh revenues to plug the nation's budget deficit, would have difficulty turning down such a generous offer.

Analysts said a marriage of Bank Austria, backed by the ruling Social Democrats, and Creditanstalt, a bastion of junior coalition partner the Conservative People's Party, would be far from harmonious.
"Looking at the way these two banks operate, I can see a Bank Austria takeover becoming a disaster," said one analyst who declined to be named.

Maxwell warned that the success of a Bank Austria takeover would depend on management willingness to reform. Bank Austria scored only limited success in integrating GiroCredit into its operations after a 1994 acquisition.
"Bank Austria will want a greater critical mass, to be a presence in Europe. Such a deal would certainly make it bigger but not necessarily more competitive," Maxwell said.
As with GiroCredit, Bank Austria will probably make big promises but close few branches, she said.
Austria's financial sector is notoriously overbanked, with every small town high street bristling with branches.
Bank Austria, with total assets of 718 billion schillings, had a market share of around 12.8 percent and 306 domestic branches at the end of last year.
Creditanstalt, with total assets of 693 billion, had a market share of 12 percent and 257 domestic branches.

"(A takeover) would be a logical move towards consolidating the banking sector but there could be a problem of integration -- they are very different houses with different management cultures," said Gerhard Auer, an analyst at ICE Securities.
Bank Austria has traditionally been a savings bank, while while Creditantalt is strong in commercial banking.
Final bids for Creditanstalt must be in by December 16. Creditanstalt ordinary shares were trading 2.15 higher at 721.65 schillings in a generally limp market. ($1=10.85 Schilling)
